newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila 1996 inflation target now seen within reach.
newsitem.headline: Manila 1996 inflation target now seen within reach.

text.p: The Philippine government appears likely to reach its full-year inflation target of at or below 8.5 percent following its announcement on Friday of the lowest monthly rate for nine years, analysts said.
The National Statistics Office said earlier that September inflation year-on-year was 4.4 percent against August's 7.9 percent and 11.3 percent in September 1995.
It said the latest figure was the lowest since July 1987.
"It's unexpectedly low after the 7.9 percent inflation rate which came out in August," said Jose Mario Cuyegkeng, research head of ING Barings Securities.

"The government inflation target becomes more achievable. It sets a positive tone for the stock market. To achieve the high end of government targets, inflation should be well within 6.0 percent in the coming months," Cuyegkeng said.
Economists, however, say the September inflation could be the bottom for the year as Christmas spending heats up in the coming months.
"Inflation could go up to 5.0 to 5.1 percent in October and 6.0 percent in December," said Ces Tanchoco, a Bank of the Philippine Islands economist.

"We're gaining confidence that October will again be lower but definitely November and December will be higher at about 7.0 percent due again to food prices," said Manuel Goseco, chief economist at Dharmala Securties Philippines.
"The 8.5 percent full-year target all of a sudden is becoming a very strong possibility. Nobody was believing it before," he said.
But University of the Philippines economist Benjamin Diokno cautioned that the September figure was exceptionally low only because last year's September figure was exceptionally high.
Inflation spiked up to 11.3 percent in September last year because a rice shortage sent prices of the staple soaring.
"The CPI in September last year was abnormally high," Professor Diokno said.

He predicted full-year inflation at 8.7 to 9.0 percent, saying increased consumer spending ahead of Christmas and the impact of the partial deregulation of the oil sector would push it above the government target.

Analysts said they expect the Philippines' benchmark 91-day Treasury bill to drop back to 11.0 percent. The rate is currently 11.593 after reaching a year-low of 11.3 last month from a year-high of 13.2 in May.
"The volatility in exchange rates in the past two or three weeks prevented the continued slide of interest rates," Cuyegkeng said.
